hero.name: Lata
hero.who: a skilled staff nurse in Mysuru whose new ward colleagues keep her at a distance

story.b: Lata has been a nurse for fifteen years, and she is good at it. When the hospital in Mysuru moves her to the children's ward, she arrives on day one with sharp eyes and high standards. By the end of the first week, she has pointed out nine mistakes. A chart filled in late. A drip stand in the wrong place. A trolley left untidy. Every correction is accurate. Yet by the third week, the other nurses go quiet when she enters the duty room. Nobody saves her a seat in the canteen. The junior nurse, Shalini, takes her questions to someone else. Lata eats her curd rice alone on a bench outside, wondering why being right feels so lonely.

ask.q: Lata is skilled and accurate, but her new colleagues keep their distance. What should she change first?
o: How she treats people, starting with more appreciation and less criticism
Nothing, since good work should be enough to earn respect
Point out mistakes more gently but just as often
ask.why: Good work alone rarely makes people warm up, and softer but constant criticism still leaves them feeling judged. Changing how she treats people, noticing what they do well and showing real interest, builds the trust her skill deserves.

chapters.take: Being right is not enough. People need to feel valued too.

story.b: One afternoon, a two-year-old in bed six screams through every attempt to give him his nebuliser. Shalini, the junior nurse, takes almost twenty minutes, but she finally gets him laughing by turning the mask into an elephant trunk. Lata watches from the station. Her first thought is that twenty minutes is too long. She almost says it. Then she stops and says something different. She tells Shalini that the elephant trick was clever, and that the boy's mother looked relieved for the first time all day. Shalini blinks, surprised. The next morning, Shalini comes to Lata with a question about a chart. She has not done that in three weeks.

ask.q: Lata's teenage son finally cleans his room, but it took him all weekend. What should she say?
o: Point out that it took far too long
Say nothing, since cleaning his room is his job anyway
Thank him for doing it and mention one specific thing he did well
ask.why: Criticism about the delay makes him defensive and less likely to try again, and silence teaches him nobody notices effort. Honest, specific appreciation makes him feel seen, and people tend to live up to the good things we notice in them.

chapters.take: Notice what people do right, and say so specifically.

story.b: Sister Mary, the senior nurse on night shifts, has barely spoken to Lata. One evening, during a quiet hour, Lata notices a faded photo stuck inside her locker door: a young woman in a nurse's cap standing outside a small village clinic. Lata asks about it. Sister Mary hesitates, then starts talking. It is her, thirty years ago, in a hill village near Madikeri, where she was the only nurse for miles. Lata listens without interrupting, asks about the walks between villages and the monsoon floods, and genuinely wants to know. They talk for forty minutes over cups of hot milk. The next week, Sister Mary quietly tells Lata which doctors prefer their reports in a particular order. It saves her hours.

ask.q: Lata's husband is starting a new job and wants his team to like him. What should she advise?
o: Tell them about his past achievements so they respect him quickly
Ask about their lives and work, and listen with real curiosity
Keep to himself until they come to him first
ask.why: Impressing people with achievements tends to create distance, and waiting quietly can look like coldness. Genuine curiosity about others makes them feel valued, and people remember how you made them feel. The interest has to be real, though, or they sense it.

chapters.take: Be curious about people. Real interest opens doors that cleverness cannot.

story.b: Lata realises she has walked past the same people every day for a month without knowing their names. The cleaner who mops the ward at six. The attender who wheels patients to X-ray. The security guard at the main gate. She starts small. She reads name badges, asks when there is none and writes the names in her pocket diary. Good morning, Kempamma. Thank you, Basavaraj. She smiles as she says it, even on tired mornings. At first they look surprised. Then they start smiling first. One night at three, a child needs to be shifted urgently and every wheelchair seems to be missing. Basavaraj appears within two minutes, pushing one he found on another floor.

ask.q: Shalini wants to feel more at home in the hospital. Which small habit would help most?
o: Learn and use the names of the people she meets daily, with a smile
Keep her head down and focus only on patients
Make friends only with the senior doctors
ask.why: Remembering someone's name and greeting them warmly tells them they matter, and it builds goodwill quickly. Keeping her head down makes her invisible, and befriending only seniors ignores the many people who keep a ward running.

chapters.take: A name remembered and a warm smile build goodwill faster than any speech.

story.b: Before Dasara, the nurses must agree on a leave rota, and the duty room gets heated. Revathi, who has worked on the ward for ten years, insists that seniors should get first choice. Lata believes a lottery is fairer, and she has good reasons. She feels the old urge to win, point by point, until Revathi goes silent. She knows how that ends. So she takes a breath. She says Revathi has a point about experience, and admits her own plan ignores who covered the last festival. Then she asks what they both want: everyone home for at least one festival day. Within twenty minutes they have a mixed plan. Revathi even offers Lata a piece of her mysore pak.

ask.q: Lata's brother-in-law posts a wrong claim in the family WhatsApp group, and she has facts to prove it. What should she do?
o: Post a long reply with links proving him wrong
Leave the group so she does not have to see it
Skip the public argument, and if it matters, talk to him privately and respectfully
ask.why: Winning a public argument usually embarrasses the other person and makes them dig in, and leaving the group cuts off the relationship. Avoiding the fight, and gently raising it in private if it truly matters, keeps the bond and often changes more minds.

chapters.take: Win the person, not the argument.

story.b: Lata has been quietly worried about shift handovers. Twice this month, the night team did not know about a child's new allergy until morning. At her old hospital, a simple bedside checklist solved this. The old Lata would have typed one up and pinned it on the wall with instructions. This time, at the weekly meeting, she just asks a question. What happened with bed four on Tuesday night, and how could we stop it happening again? The room goes quiet. Then Shalini says maybe they need a short list to go through at each bed. Revathi adds that allergies should go at the top. Lata nods and asks Shalini to design it. Within a week, everyone uses Shalini's checklist.

ask.q: Lata's ward in-charge wants staff to start using a new digital chart, but they resist. What would work best?
o: Order them to use it from Monday and check daily
Ask questions that help them see the benefit, and let them shape how it is used
Explain all its features in a long presentation
ask.why: People resist ideas pushed on them, so orders and long presentations often harden resistance. Asking questions that let them discover the benefit, and giving them a hand in shaping it, turns the change into their own idea, and then they support it.

chapters.take: People support ideas they help create. Let them own it.

story.h: A seat saved in the canteen
story.b: By the end of winter, the children's ward feels different to Lata. Her standards have not dropped at all. She still notices every late chart. But now she thanks people first and asks questions more often than she corrects. Shalini brings her every tricky case, and Sister Mary has taught her the shortcuts of the night shift. Kempamma and Basavaraj greet her before she greets them. The ward next door has copied Shalini's checklist. One afternoon Lata walks into the canteen with her tiffin and finds Revathi waving, a chair already pulled out beside her. Lata sits down and laughs at a story about Revathi's grandson. She does not eat lunch alone anymore.

chapters.take: Warmth did not lower her standards. It got people to share them.
